questions.enonce_markdown: The real valued function $f$ is defined as $f: x \mapsto \dfrac{4x}{x - 1}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 1$. Show that $f$ is injective. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A function is injective (one-to-one) if $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ implies $x_1 = x_2$ for all $x_1, x_2$ in the domain.

Let $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}$ with $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$:
$$\frac{4x_1}{x_1 - 1} = \frac{4x_2}{x_2 - 1}.$$
Both denominators are non-zero, so cross-multiply:
$$4x_1(x_2 - 1) = 4x_2(x_1 - 1) \;\Rightarrow\; 4x_1x_2 - 4x_1 = 4x_1x_2 - 4x_2 \;\Rightarrow\; -4x_1 = -4x_2 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 = x_2.$$
Hence $f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2$, so $f$ is injective. $\blacksquare$

(Alternative: $f(x) = 4 + \dfrac{4}{x - 1}$, and $f'(x) = -\dfrac{4}{(x-1)^2} < 0$ on each branch; $f$ takes the value $4$ never, and values above $4$ only for $x > 1$ and below $4$ only for $x < 1$, so no value is repeated.)

questions.enonce_markdown: The real valued function $f$ is defined as $f: x \mapsto \dfrac{4x}{x - 1}$, $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 1$. Find $(f \circ f)(x)$, stating its domain. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The composite.** $(f \circ f)(x) = f(f(x))$ with $f(x) = \dfrac{4x}{x-1}$:
$$f(f(x)) = \frac{4\cdot\dfrac{4x}{x-1}}{\dfrac{4x}{x-1} - 1} = \frac{\dfrac{16x}{x-1}}{\dfrac{4x - (x-1)}{x-1}} = \frac{16x}{3x + 1}.$$
$$\boxed{(f \circ f)(x) = \frac{16x}{3x + 1}}$$

**The domain.** For $f(f(x))$ to exist we need
- $x$ in the domain of the inner function: $x \neq 1$;
- $f(x)$ in the domain of the outer function: $f(x) \neq 1$. Now $\dfrac{4x}{x-1} = 1 \iff 4x = x - 1 \iff x = -\dfrac13$, so $x \neq -\dfrac13$.

$$\boxed{\text{Domain of } f \circ f = \left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq 1,\ x \neq -\tfrac13\right\} = \mathbb{R} \setminus \left\{1, -\tfrac13\right\}}$$

Note that the simplified formula $\dfrac{16x}{3x+1}$ alone would only forbid $x = -\frac13$; the value $x = 1$ must also be excluded because $f(1)$ is not defined.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two statements $p$ and $q$ are given by:

$p$: The principal goes to the ministry.

$q$: The principal will meet the minister.

Write out the following propositions in ordinary English:

(a) $p \wedge q$,

(b) $\sim p \vee \sim q$,

(c) $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The symbols mean: $\wedge$ = "and", $\vee$ = "or", $\sim$ = "not", $\Rightarrow$ = "implies" ("if ... then").

(a) $p \wedge q$: **The principal goes to the ministry and (the principal) will meet the minister.**

(b) $\sim p \vee \sim q$: **The principal does not go to the ministry or the principal will not meet the minister.**

(c) $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q$: **If the principal does not go to the ministry, then the principal will not meet the minister.**

(Remark: by De Morgan's law, (b) is the negation of (a): $\sim(p \wedge q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q$.)
